content_summary.bibliographic: SSRN working paper, abstract_id 7417258; DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7417258; published 2026 (Crossref indexed 14 September 2026; the exact posting day and the 21-page length come from the scanner note, not from any record fetched here); authors Alex Fernandez (Granada), Rowan Arundel (Amsterdam), Ricardo Duque-Calvache (Granada). Not peer reviewed as of this check.
abstract_verbatim_key_sentences (Crossre: "In Spain, the Impuesto sobre Bienes Inmuebles (IBI) is levied on registered cadastral values that are revised infrequently and at uneven intervals, so the effective base departs from market value in ways that are neither uniform nor neutral across households."
"Drawing on Henry George's concept of land rent, this paper examines how increases in land value are captured by particular households across urban Spain."
"The final simulations suggest that reorienting taxation towards property and away from labour has the potential to improve progressivity and reduce disparities in housing wealth."
content_summary.research_design_as_stated_in_abstract: (1) Data: 'newly available household-level registry data' (the registry is not named in the abstract; whether it is Catastro, Registradores or tax-agency data is NOT known). (2) Method: 'a simplified asset pricing model'. Step one 'tests for vertical inequity in the cadastral base across urban Spain'. Step two 'builds a microsimulation to estimate the capitalised value of the resulting tax saving and to trace its distribution across housing wealth, income, age and location', alongside 'a stylised income-tax-linked scheme for recycling the additional revenue'. Cities, period, the measure of undertaxation (effective IBI rate vs assessment-to-market ratios by value decile) and tenure/owner-type breakdowns are NOT in the abstract.
content_summary.authors_own_findings_vs_cited_figures: The abstract reports no numeric finding. The only result-like statement is the hedged simulation headline above ('suggest ... has the potential to improve progressivity and reduce disparities in housing wealth'), which is the authors' own simulation output, not a measured outcome. The abstract's background sentence ('Existing research has identified land appreciation as a central driver of wealth accumulation') is attributed to unnamed prior literature; the authors' own related evidence is Arundel, Torrado & Duque-Calvache (2024), who found rising spatial polarisation of Spanish housing-value accumulation with expensive areas gaining more in absolute terms and in appreciation rates (EPA, abstract read). No claim about WHO benefits by value decile, tenure or owner type can be reported until the body is read. The scanner note's phrasing ('who gains when urban property is systematically undertaxed') presupposes the finding; the abstract only says the test for vertical inequity is run.
content_summary.policy_conclusion_per_abstract: Shift taxation toward property and away from labour; recycle revenue through the income tax. Framed explicitly with Henry George's land-rent concept, which makes this a rare mainstream-academic housing paper that invokes George in its own abstract (a notable fact for this wiki, but the abstract alone does not show how heavily the paper leans on George).

tier1_primaries_for_the_spanish_system (.valor_catastral_definition: RDL 1/2004 (Ley del Catastro Inmobiliario) art. 22: cadastral value is determined objectively from Catastro data and is the sum of the land (suelo) value and the construction value. Land and building are separately valued in the cadastral base, which matters for any land-only reform design.
tier1_primaries_for_the_spanish_system (.market-value ceiling: RDL 1/2004 art. 23.2 (Spanish): 'El valor catastral de los inmuebles no podra superar el valor de mercado ...' with a 'coeficiente de referencia al mercado' fixed by ministerial order. The statute therefore sets cadastral value as a ceiling at or below market value by design. The numeric coefficient (commonly cited as 0.5) lives in a ministerial order that was NOT fetched; do not state 0.5 without reading that order.
tier1_primaries_for_the_spanish_system (.revaluation_mechanism: RDL 1/2004 art. 24: values set by municipal 'ponencias de valores' (collective revaluations); art. 32: the annual State Budget Law may update cadastral values by coefficients, and municipalities may request them only if at least five years have passed since the last general collective revaluation and market divergence is substantial (request to the Direccion General del Catastro by 31 May). This is the legal source of 'revised infrequently and at uneven intervals'.
tier1_primaries_for_the_spanish_system (.ibi_base_and_rates: RDL 2/2004 (TRLRHL) art. 65: the IBI base is the cadastral value. Art. 72: statutory urban rate band 0.4% (minimum/default) to 1.10% (maximum), rural 0.3% to 0.90%; municipalities may add percentage points (0.07 for provincial and autonomous-community capitals, 0.07 where surface public transport runs, 0.06 for extra municipal services) and may differentiate rates for non-residential uses on the top 10% of cadastral values; since the 2023 housing law, municipalities may surcharge permanently vacant residential property by up to 50% (100% after three years, with further points for owners of two or more vacant units).
tier1_primaries_for_the_spanish_system (.transition_smoothing: RDL 2/2004 arts. 67-68: after a general revaluation the increase in taxable base is phased in over nine years through a declining reduction coefficient (0.9 in year one, falling 0.1 a year). A designed lag that sustains the gap between assessed and market value after every revaluation.
tier1_primaries_for_the_spanish_system (.oecd_revenue_statistics_4100: Spain: recurrent taxes on immovable property = 0.89% of GDP in 2024 (1.08% in 2019, 1.13% in 2021, 0.93% in 2023) and 2.43% of total taxation in 2024; 99.8% of it local government (0.888% of GDP of 0.890%). In euros the revenue was about EUR 13.5bn in 2019 and EUR 14.2bn in 2024: nominally almost flat for five years, so its GDP share fell. That pattern is consistent with a base indexed only by occasional coefficients, but the OECD series alone cannot show cause (rate cuts and municipal choices are confounders). OECD SDMX dataflow DF_RSGLOBAL v2.1 (flagged NonProductionDataflow in the API metadata), series T_4100, sector S13; saved as oecd-rsglobal-4100.csv; the edition label (Revenue Statistics 2025 vs a later release) is not stated in the API response and must be confirmed against the OECD publication.

uncertainties: Full text never read: the body may qualify, contradict or quantify the abstract's claims. In particular the abstract does not say whether the vertical-inequity test found regressivity (higher-value homes assessed at lower fractions of market value), progressivity, or no pattern. Do not write either on the wiki.

The 'household-level registry data' source and coverage (which cities, which years, whether cadastral values are matched to transaction prices or to self-reported values) are unknown; 'urban Spain' is the abstract's phrase.

'Simplified asset pricing model' means capitalised value of the tax saving is a modelled quantity under assumed discount rates and horizon, not an observed price effect; wiki pages must call it a simulation.

The paper's land/building split is unknown: Spanish cadastral values separate land and construction (RDL 1/2004 art. 22), so a land-only counterfactual is feasible, but the abstract talks about 'land and property underassessment' and a shift 'towards property', which may not be land-only.
The scanner note gives posting date 14 September 2026 and 21 pages; the only machine-readable dates are year 2026 (Crossref) and index time 2026-09-14; page count unconfirmed.
Peer-review status: working paper; may change on publication. Re-check for a journal version before relying on any number.

verdict: ENRICH from the OECD primary, not from the tracker. Do not cite the Tax Foundation tracker as a source on the wiki. Specific enrichments: places/united-kingdom.md (re-anchor the '2.8% of GDP' figure to OECD Revenue Statistics 4100, 2024 = 2.80%, and correct 'second in the OECD only to Canada': in the OECD series the UK is first among all 36-38 members with data in 2022, 2023 and 2024); places/estonia.md (OECD 4100: 0.15% of GDP, 0.41% of total taxation in 2024, about EUR 58m a year; check the page's 'significant source of local government revenue' wording); places/germany.md (0.37% of GDP in 2024 beside the Baden-Wurttemberg section); and the proposed places/spain.md (0.89% of GDP). The tracker adds only two items not already on the wiki or in the OECD data (Croatia's new 2025 recurrent property tax; the tracker's own claim that Estonia alone taxes only land) and neither warrants citing it.
claim_grade: A-claim for the OECD figures (official statistical series, Tier 1: OECD). The tracker itself is a derived compilation: B/C-grade, Tier 2 under section 4c (think-tank staff). The tracker's normative statements (e.g. Estonia's property tax 'is the most efficient') are interpretive (D-claim) and advocacy from a free-market think tank.

author_tier_judgment.Tax Foundation: Think tank (non-profit, free-market oriented); not an official or standing body, not a peer-reviewed venue. Tier 2 under section 4c: may be named as the compiler of a tracker, never as support. Not listed in people-tiers.json.
author_tier_judgment.Alex Mengden: Economist at Tax Foundation Europe (BA philosophy and economics, Bayreuth; MSc economics, LMU Munich per the tracker's author box). Staff of a think tank with no peer-reviewed record visible on the page: Tier 2. Judged by the rubric.
author_tier_judgment.primary_data_owner: OECD Revenue Statistics (category 4100) is Tier 1 (official standing body). IMF Investment and Capital Stock Dataset is Tier 1 for the denominator. 'Recent Changes' paragraph: from 2025 Germany devolves its property tax base to states; Baden-Wurttemberg 'apply property taxes only to the value of land'; 'Croatia introduced a recurrent property tax in 2025, levied on the square metres of land and floor area.' It states the incentive logic in generic terms: 'high property taxes levied not only on land but also on buildings and structures can also discourage investment' (intro to the 'Ideally, property taxes ...' block; paraphrase, wording not copied beyond this clause).

content_summary.land_only_countries_check: Tracker: Estonia is the only land-only tax. Wiki: Estonia land-only since 1993 (places/estonia.md); Denmark grundskyld is 'separate from and in addition to' a building tax (places/denmark.md); Fernandez Milan, Kapfer & Creutzig (2016) score eight European countries' land/location taxes (Denmark, Lithuania, Slovakia, Estonia, Austria, Hungary, Italy, Romania, plus Slovenia abolished). So the tracker CONFIRMS Estonia as the single pure land-only recurrent property tax and does not CONFLICT with the wiki, but its 'Tax on Real Property' label (from PwC) hides that Denmark, Lithuania and others also levy separate land taxes alongside building taxes. The wiki should state 'Estonia taxes land only; Denmark and Lithuania levy separate land taxes alongside building or property taxes' and cite statutes or Fernandez Milan et al., not the tracker. Latvia: the wiki holds no claim that Latvia has a land tax; its OECD 4100 yield (0.59% of GDP, 1.68% of total taxation) is far above Estonia's.
content_summary.oecd_4100_is_not_land_value_tax: The wiki already states on research/oecd-taxation-economic-growth.md that OECD category 4100 covers land and buildings together; the tracker's figures inherit that limit and add nothing on the land share.

existing_wiki_coverage.cites_tax_foundation: Only research/digital-services-taxes.md, research/digital-services-tax-incidence.md, research/maryland-digital-ad-tax.md, concepts/taxing-tech-rents.md and objections/taxing-quasi-rents-kills-innovation.md (digital-services-tax context). No page cites a Tax Foundation property-tax tracker.
existing_wiki_coverage.oecd_4100_on_the_wiki: research/oecd-taxation-economic-growth.md and research/arnold-tax-growth-ej.md use category 4100 only for the Johansson et al. growth ranking and note it is land plus buildings. No page cites a country-by-country OECD Revenue Statistics 4100 table. Figures stated without a primary anchor: places/united-kingdom.md ('about 2.8% of GDP from annual property taxes, second in the OECD only to Canada; ... 3.7% with stamp duties', sourced via the Tier 2 Henry George Foundation essay); research/india-mohua-value-capture-framework.md ('OECD average of 1.1% of GDP'); research/lincoln-institute-latam-property-tax-book.md ('OECD's 1%+ average'). The OECD series gives UK 2.80% (matches) but UK is first, not second, in 2022-2024 (2.84, 2.78, 2.80 vs Canada 2.69, 2.69, 2.64; Canada was higher only in 2021: 2.92 vs 2.83). The '3.7% with stamp duties' figure was not checked.
existing_wiki_coverage.land_only_countries: places/estonia.md (land tax on land value only since 1993; says the tax 'is a significant source of local government revenue' without a figure), places/denmark.md (grundskyld, plus the Fernandez Milan 11/20 score), research/fernandez-milan-location-value-taxes.md (eight European location-value taxes scored on 2014 data), places/germany.md (Baden-Wurttemberg Bodenwertsteuer from January 2025: area x Bodenrichtwert, 1.3 per mille reduced 30% to 0.91 per mille for residential; Bundesfinanzhof ruling 20 May 2026). The tracker's Baden-Wurttemberg note is already covered on the wiki from the Bundesfinanzhof press release and state guides (stronger sources). Lithuania and Latvia: no wiki page on their land taxes; Lithuania appears in the Fernandez Milan page (score 8/20) and Raslanas et al. valuation case; Latvia only as the Riga comparator in Tomson (2016) and as a repealed-ACE country.
existing_wiki_coverage.european_comparisons_in_place_pages: places/netherlands.md has no property-tax figures (land-value-capture focus). places/germany.md has no revenue figures. places/united-kingdom.md has the only cross-country statistic (above). There is no Spain page and no page tabulating European recurrent property taxation.
existing_wiki_coverage.croatia_2025_tax: Not on the wiki (Croatia appears as ACE country and in Kilic et al. 2019).

uncertainties: OECD Revenue Statistics edition not identified: the SDMX response does not label the edition and the OECD landing pages were blocked. The 2024 values are very likely provisional in the latest edition; confirm in the published edition before citing a 2024 number.

The SDMX dataflow is marked NonProductionDataflow in its metadata; values matched the tracker's cited source (category 4100) and the UK's 2.8% in the wiki, but confirm against the OECD Data Explorer view or the Revenue Statistics country notes before publication.
The tracker's capital-stock ratios depend on the IMF series (not fetched); the wiki should not republish them.

The country coverage of 'OECD' in my ranking check: 38 members present for 2022-2023, 36 for 2024 (Australia and Greece missing); a 'highest in the OECD' sentence should say 'among the OECD countries with data'.
Denmark 2024 break and Czechia 2024 jump (0.16% to 0.29% of GDP) are unexplained and may be revisions or reforms.

Whether the Estonia page's 'significant' wording is right is untested: 0.15% of GDP and 0.41% of total taxation nationally, but local-government share unknown; a reasonable T1 check is Estonian local-government revenue statistics (Statistics Estonia), not done here.
The tracker's statement that Estonia is the 'sole' land-only tax rests on PwC summaries, not statute; do not repeat it as the wiki's own claim without a legal source.

recommendation_on_citing_the_tracker: Do not cite it. It (a) is Tier 2, (b) re-expresses OECD data in a non-standard denominator, (c) carries visible unit errors in earlier vintages, and (d) takes its land/building classification from PwC marketing summaries. Everything of value in it is reproducible from the OECD source it names. If the wiki ever wants capital-stock ratios, it should compute them itself from OECD and IMF data and cite those two.
